sections.h2: What does a Lebanon seller need to understand first?
sections.html:
Lebanon packs about 26,500 people into a small grid of older homes, many of them rented, with a typical owner's home valued at $156,500. That price level means repairs, taxes and closing costs take a large share of any sale, so the details below are worth reading before you set a price.

The city is also Lebanon County's seat of government, 26 miles east of Harrisburg and 88 miles northwest of Philadelphia. It covers just 4.17 square miles, which works out to about 6,435 people per square mile. The Census Bureau's mid-2025 figure is 26,479, a 1.1 percent drop from 2020. The city had gained 5.2 percent in the previous decade.

A Lebanon owner can use a broker, post the sign personally or take a cash bid for the house. In every case the deed is filed at the courthouse on South 8th Street, and the county treasurer keeps the tax payment records.

sections.h2: How did Lebanon become the city it is?
sections.html:
George Steitz founded the town in 1740 under the name Steitztown. Settlers arrived about 1720, streets were laid out in 1753, a borough charter came in 1821, and city status followed on November 25, 1885. Population passed 14,000 by 1890 and peaked at 30,045 in 1960 before sliding to 24,461 in 2000.

Manufacturing built much of the housing. The Union Canal ran along the north side from 1828 to 1885, San Giorgio pasta has been made here since 1914, and a large Bethlehem Steel mill once operated in the city. Lebanon bologna, first made here before the 1780s, still carries the city's name. The Quittapahilla Creek drains the city westward toward the Susquehanna.

  • Neighboring municipalities: North Lebanon, South Lebanon, West Lebanon and North Cornwall townships.
  • Schools: the Lebanon School District, which serves the city and West Lebanon Township, plus a Harrisburg Area Community College campus and the Lebanon County Career and Technology Center.
  • Weather: about 46 inches of precipitation and 24 inches of snow in a typical year, with January averaging about 30 degrees and July about 74. Gutters, roofs and basements on older homes get tested every winter.

sections.h2: How do Lebanon homes show up in Census data?
sections.html:
Lebanon has more renters than owners, lower incomes than the state's suburbs and a younger, more diverse population. Most homes here are rented, so landlords make up a big part of both the selling and the buying side.

With rent near $992 against a $156,500 home value, the rental market is a major buyer of Lebanon houses. A seller of a tenant-occupied property should expect investors to ask for the rent roll, the license and the last inspection results.

sections.h2: What are the City of Lebanon's rental license rules?
sections.html:
Every dwelling unit or rooming unit offered for rent in the city must be licensed, and each parcel with rental units needs its own application. The rules matter to a seller because a buyer inherits the license history.

  • A $25 penalty is added every 60 days a fee stays unpaid after billing.
  • Renewal is delayed or denied if money is owed to the city or code violations are open.
  • The owner must keep a contract with a licensed trash hauler on file, and a property manager must be within 20 miles of the city limit.
  • Grass and weeds cannot exceed 12 inches, snow and ice must come off sidewalks within 24 hours after a snowfall ends, and inoperable or unlicensed vehicles cannot sit on a premises more than 5 days.
  • Smoke alarms and carbon monoxide detectors are required, and a license revoked for unsafe conditions costs $100 to reinstate.

Questions go to the city's code enforcement office at 717-639-2800, option 2, at 735 Cumberland Street. For a rental, get copies of the current license and any violation notice into your file before you answer a buyer.

sections.h2: What permits and zoning rules can slow a Lebanon sale?
sections.html:
The city's Building and Zoning Division, part of Public Works, runs permits and zoning. A zoning permit is required for building or altering a structure, adding an addition, demolishing or moving one, and putting up fences, decks, sheds and garages. It is also required for a change of use, a swimming pool or hot tub deeper than 18 inches, and a sign.

Construction inspections are done by outside code inspection firms under contract, and the city asks for at least 24 hours' notice. A deck or shed that an earlier owner added without a permit is something an inspector may catch. Settle that question before listing, or ask the zoning office what the city would require.

The city zoning ordinance defines 10 districts. A Zoning Hearing Board hears variance and special exception requests.

sections.h2: How do county taxes and the Tax Claim Bureau affect a Lebanon sale?
sections.html:
The Lebanon County Treasurer collects the county real estate tax, the city tax and, now, the Lebanon City School District bill, so one office can tell you whether anything is owed on a city parcel. The Tax Claim Bureau charges $15 per parcel for a tax certification, and a mailed request must include a stamped return envelope.

Delinquent taxes pass to the Tax Claim Bureau each January. The owner is sent a certified letter showing the balance, interest and costs, along with the date to pay in order to avoid a sale. About 17 months after that first notice the bureau mails a notice of sale. Buyers at the upset sale take the property subject to judgments, liens and mortgages, and bidders must pre-register for a $25 fee. The 2026 upset sale list set the sale date for October 12, 2026, and that date has passed.

A seller behind on taxes should pay or arrange the balance before closing. Once a property is on the sale list, the process follows a fixed bureau and court calendar.

sections.h2: How are assessments appealed and the deed recorded in Lebanon County?
sections.html:
The county's rules set September 1 as the yearly filing date for assessment appeals, with a 4:30 closing time at the Board of Assessment Revision. A notice that arrives late waits for the following year. The filing fee for a residential property of one to four units is $50 and is not refunded. You or an authorized representative must attend the hearing, and the board can raise, lower or keep the assessment.

Filings go to the Assessment Office at 400 South 8th Street, Room 118. The county also lets owners view their records free on DataScout, using the control number and web password printed on the tax bill.

The Recorder of Deeds is in Room 107 of the same courthouse, open on weekdays, and accepts cash or check only. Most documents come back the following business day, and the Assessment Office must certify the parcel identifier before a deed records. The state transfer tax is 1 percent, and the recorder's office adds any local share when it collects.

sections.h2: Which Lebanon houses suit a cash offer?
sections.html:
A cash sale suits a house with heavy repairs, a rental carrying open code items, a vacant building or an estate. It is also useful when tax delinquency puts the house on a calendar you cannot move.

Price comparison matters here because the median value is modest. Add up the commission, repairs, transfer tax and months of ownership on a listing, and compare that net with a cash figure. To ask for an offer on a Lebanon house in its present state, contact Cash Home Buyers.

faqs.q: Does Lebanon require a rental license?
faqs.a: Yes. Every dwelling unit or rooming unit offered for rent in the City of Lebanon must be licensed, with a separate application for each parcel that has rental units.

faqs.q: When are Lebanon County assessment appeals due?
faqs.a: September 1 each year, filed with the Board of Assessment Revision at the Assessment Office on South 8th Street. A residential appeal costs $50.

faqs.q: How long can Lebanon County delinquent taxes sit before a sale?
faqs.a: Unpaid taxes move to the Tax Claim Bureau every January, and owners have until the last working day of the next June. A notice of sale follows about 17 months after the first notice.

faqs.q: Where is a Lebanon deed recorded?
faqs.a: At the Lebanon County Recorder of Deeds, Room 107 of the courthouse at 400 South 8th Street. The office takes cash or check and can also accept electronic recording.

faqs.q: Which school district serves the City of Lebanon?
faqs.a: The Lebanon School District, which covers the city and West Lebanon Township. The county treasurer now collects its tax bill for city parcels.
